Axis Robotics: Turning Internet Users Into Robot Trainers

I first came across Axis Robotics through crypto.

But after spending some time reading through the product and its research, the thing that caught my attention wasn’t the token side.

It was a much simpler question:

AI had the internet to learn from. What do robots learn from?

ChatGPT has mountains of text. Image models have millions of pictures.

A robot that needs to learn how to pick up a cup, open a drawer, organize objects, or use a tool needs something very different: data about actions in the physical world.

And that kind of data is expensive.

The traditional way of collecting it involves real robots, real environments, operators, hardware maintenance, and a lot of time. Every additional task or setup adds more cost.

Axis Robotics is trying another approach.

You open a browser, enter a simulated environment, receive a task, and control a virtual robot to complete it.

No robot required. No expensive setup.

Every successful attempt creates a trajectory — essentially a record of how the task was completed, including things like robot movements, observations, states, and actions.

So when you move a robotic arm toward an object, grab it, and place it in the right location, you’re leaving behind an example of how a human would solve that task.

That example can later become training data.

On the surface, it almost looks like a browser game.

The problem behind it is much more serious.

Earlier this year, Axis reported that roughly 18,000 users generated close to 100,000 trajectories across 27 task types in just five days.

By the end of April, the project said it had reached around 45,000 registered users and more than 500,000 trajectories.

It crossed 1 million trajectories in June.

By early July, Axis was reporting roughly 1.6 million.

Its website now says the network has grown beyond 100,000 contributors.

Those numbers sound impressive.

But I don’t think the number of trajectories is the most important part.

In robotics, more data doesn’t automatically mean better data.

A clean demonstration that solves a difficult task can be far more useful than hundreds of repetitive or poorly executed attempts.

Diversity matters too.

Different objects. Different camera angles. Different layouts. Different mistakes. Different ways of recovering when something goes wrong.

That’s where Axis becomes more interesting.

The team isn’t simply collecting raw demonstrations. Their pipeline includes validation, filtering, trajectory processing, task generation, and simulation-based augmentation.

There’s also some early research behind the idea.

In July 2026, the Axis team published a paper on arXiv titled “AXIS: A Growable Community-Driven Data Engine for Scalable Robot Manipulation.”

The research dataset contained more than 50,000 trajectories across 207 tasks.

When the researchers continued training the π0.5 robotics model with AXIS data, they reported an improvement in overall task success, with some of the clearer gains appearing under changes to camera positions, layouts, and sensor noise.

That doesn’t prove Axis has solved the robotics data problem.

It’s still a preprint, and moving from simulation to reliable real-world robots remains brutally difficult.

But at least there’s something measurable behind the story.

And recently, Axis changed the way humans contribute.

With Axis V2, the human doesn’t necessarily control the robot for the entire task anymore.

The AI policy tries first.

The contributor watches.

When the model starts making a mistake, the human steps in, corrects it, and lets the model continue.

Imagine the robot can already complete 80% of a task correctly.

There’s little reason for a human to repeat that 80%.

The valuable part may be the remaining 20% — the exact moment where the model gets confused.

That creates a pretty interesting loop:

model attempts task → model fails → human corrects it → new data is created → model trains again

And then the process repeats.

That loop is probably the part of @axisrobotics I’m most interested in following.

Crypto enters the picture because Axis needs a large network of people to generate, correct, and evaluate this data.

But even if you completely ignore the token side, the main question is still there:

Can data created by thousands of people inside simulations actually make real robots meaningfully better?

If the answer eventually turns out to be yes, Axis could become an interesting piece of infrastructure for Physical AI.

If not, millions of trajectories may end up being little more than a nice-looking number on a dashboard.

For now, I’m still digging.

Next: what does an Axis contributor actually do, and where does your data go after you hit Submit on @KaitoAI ?

Announcing our new Speech Agent Arena, evaluating Speech to Speech models on real-world scenarios to analyze conversational preference and task success rate

Existing Speech to Speech benchmarks cover reasoning, simulated agentic tasks, and conversational dynamics such as turn-taking and interruption handling. The Speech Agent Arena compares models and cascaded systems as humans complete real-world tasks, measuring conversational preference and successful tool use. This allows us to provide an evaluation which closer reflects real-world use, offering insight into which models users most prefer speaking with and how effectively those models support their requests.

Overview of the Speech Agent Arena and Task Success Rate
Human participants compare two hidden Speech to Speech models on the same assigned scenario, one of 15 agentic scenarios (tasks requiring tool calling, such as ordering takeout) or 20 non-agentic scenarios (tasks without tool calling, such as asking about opening hours). After separate live conversations with each model, participants select which they preferred, with these pairwise votes used to fit a Preference Elo score. For agentic scenarios, Task Success Rate is the share of eligible conversations (no participant deviations or unverifiable cases) where the model completed the requested action through the correct final tool call or calls.

For all but a New Patient Dental Booking example, scenario model prompts, tool schemas and participant instructions are currently private to reduce overfitting. Additionally, the Speech Agent Arena currently uses a qualified pool of paid, screened third-party participants to conduct and evaluate agent interactions.

Key results:
➤ Arena Preference Elo: @GoogleAI Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Preview - Minimal leads at 1,046 Elo, followed by Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Preview - High at 1,014, @OpenAI GPT-Realtime-1.5 at 1,000, GPT Realtime (Aug '25) at 944, and @ElevenLabs Agents (default cascaded system of Scribe v2 Realtime / GPT-4o Mini / Eleven v3, with pre-registered tool schema) at 937. In reviewed conversations, highly preferred models tended to respond quickly, sound more natural and produce fewer unnatural sounds or audio artifacts
➤ Task Success Rate: @SpaceXAI Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High leads at 94.7%, followed by @OpenAI GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at 91.5%, @ElevenLabs Agents (Default Cascaded System) at 90.5%, and GPT-Realtime-2 (High) at 89.8%, with GPT Realtime (Aug '25) and GPT-Realtime-2.1 Minimal tied at 89.4%. Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Preview - Minimal leads overall preference at 1,046 Elo but records a 74.6% Task Success Rate, showing that a preferred conversation does not always result in successful task completion - some conversations can sound as though the requested action was completed even when the required final tool call was unsuccessful

We are continuing to expand our coverage of native and cascaded Speech to Speech systems, and welcome feedback as we add more models, providers and scenarios.

Physical AI has a data problem. LLMs had the entire internet to learn from. Robots don’t have that luxury.

A robot learning to grasp an object, pour water or navigate a room needs much more than videos. It needs actual action data ~ movement, positioning, contact forces, joint states and 6-DoF poses.

Collecting all of this in the real world is expensive, slow and difficult to scale.

This is the problem @axisrobotics is trying to solve.

The idea is surprisingly simple:

-> Open Axis in your browser
-> Connect your wallet
-> Control a simulated robotic arm
-> Complete tasks almost like playing a game
-> Every successful task becomes a verified data trajectory
-> Those trajectories can be used to build datasets for Physical AI
-> Contributors are rewarded on Base

But the part I find interesting isn't really the game.
It's the distribution model behind it.

Traditional teleoperation requires physical robots, workstations and human operators. If you want 10x more data, you basically need significantly more hardware and labor.

@axisrobotics is trying to change that equation.
Instead of bringing humans to robots, they bring simulated robots to humans through the browser.
Potentially thousands of contributors can generate different trajectories from different environments without owning a robot themselves.

And simulation solves another important problem. Internet video might show a robotic arm picking up a cup, but the video doesn't naturally give a model all the underlying information about forces, joints and precise spatial movement required to reproduce that action.

Simulation can.

My bet is that robotics data networks will become much more important over the next few years.

Compute is becoming easier to access and models will continue improving, but useful Physical AI still needs enormous amounts of diverse interaction data. The projects that figure out how to collect that data cheaply and at global scale could end up owning a very valuable layer of the robotics stack. That’s why I’m following Axis. Today it looks like a browser game where you control virtual robots.

Long term, I think the more interesting question is whether @axisrobotics can turn thousands of people doing these tasks into a continuously growing data engine for Physical AI.

If they can, the game is just the interface. The dataset is the real product.

One AI training task tells a company almost nothing about you

It takes hundreds before they can trust you at all
A single voice clip, gameplay session, or preference ranking can't prove you're consistent, careful, or reliable

Only a pattern across many contributions can show that

The problem is most platforms only track that pattern inside one task category

Switch to a different type of work and your history resets to zero, even though you're the same contributor

@KGeN_IO takes a different approach
> It treats reputation as one continuous profile instead of something that resets per task. Gameplay, voice data, social activity,
all of it feeds into the same identity instead of living in separate silos

The scoring itself breaks into five parts:
proof you're human, proof of consistency, proof of skill, proof of economic participation, and proof of network. Each one measures something different, but they combine into a single score that travels with you across every task type you touch,

That reputation layer isn't just theoretical
It's the same infrastructure Humyn Labs is building on for its Proof of Expert system, which sources verified human data to train AI models

So the more you contribute on KGeN, the stronger your standing gets everywhere that reputation is used, not just in the specific task where you earned it.

That's a meaningfully different definition of "putting in the work" than most Web3 platforms operate on. Most systems treat every task as its own isolated transaction: you show up, you deliver, you get paid, and your history doesn't follow you anywhere else

KGeN is betting that reputation should compound instead of reset, the same way trust works between actual people

Whether that bet pays off depends on adoption outside KGeN's own ecosystem
A portable reputation score is only as valuable as the number of platforms willing to read and respect it, Right now that list includes @Teamhumynlabs , but the real test is whether more AI labs and Web3 platforms start treating this as a standard rather than a nice to have

Should reputation always carry over like this, or does it make more sense for platforms to reset per task type?

Tarun on how AI training evolved from pre-training to self generating harnesses and why data costs are catching up to compute

"Let's take a tiny history lesson. In 2023, with stable diffusion and GPT-3, it was just bigger is better, pre-training. Then in 2024 it was directed RL, how you feed the data after training, this in context learning type of stuff, which got you another order of magnitude performance increase across a lot of evals and practical use cases"

"Then the harness thing was, if you customize how you do the RL for different applications, you get even better performance versus a generic RL environment. And the current meta-harness, the generic can answer anything, Claude Code or Codex type of thing, which arguably is what killed Cursor and why I'd argue they ended up doing the acquisition, that can figure out which environment to use just in time"

"The problem with this environment stuff from a data consumption perspective is you now have to pay a lot more for annotated data to customize the different environments. That's why people have been talking about data cost coming close to matching compute cost for training, because you need much more annotated data for each specific task domain"

"The belief is that once one of these things is good enough, instead of having to get data this way and generating synthetic data via RL, the model can generate the harness in real time"

I made a quick video showing the process step by step.

1. Open Axis
2. Choose a task
3. Control the virtual robot
4. Complete the required action
5. Submit & sign your contribution on Base

Your completed task generates a trajectory that contributes to Physical AI training data.
